video_metadata.title: China’s New AI Robots Just Broke The Human Skill Barrier
video_metadata.description:
This week in robotics got kind of ridiculous. South Korea showed off a humanoid that can run, jump, play soccer, and moonwalk, China pushed humanoids deeper into tennis, sprinting, and human-like motion, and UBTech is now aiming to mass-produce 10,000 humanoid robots with Siemens. On top of that, a restaurant robot caused chaos in public, another robot reads human brain signals to stop mistakes before they happen, and new breakthroughs in biohybrid robots, compostable soft robots, and robotic hands made the whole week feel way more serious than usual.

✉ General Inquiries: airevolutionofficial@gmail.com

🧠 What You’ll See

3:05 WANDER-bot Wind Robot
SOURCE: https://www.cranfield.ac.uk/press/news-2026/wind-powered-robot-could-enable-long-term-exploration-of-hostile-environments
4:21 Haidilao Robot Chaos
SOURCE: https://abc7news.com/post/viral-video-dancing-robot-restrained-staff-cupertino-restaurant-haidilao-hot-pot-causing-chaos/18736333/
5:36 LATENT Tennis Robot
SOURCE: https://zzk273.github.io/LATENT/
7:03 Bolt Sprint Humanoid
SOURCE: https://hic.zju.edu.cn/hicenglish/2026/0204/c82671a3132666/page.htm
8:14 OstraBot Muscle Swimmer
SOURCE: https://news.nus.edu.sg/what-a-flex-swimming-robot/
9:27 UBTech Siemens Robot Push
SOURCE: https://www.sz.gov.cn/en_szgov/business/news/content/post_12689428.html
10:34 Brain Signal Robot Control
SOURCE: https://news.okstate.edu/articles/engineering-architecture-technology/2026/osu_research_uses_brain_signals_to_improve_robot_decision_making
11:49 Compostable Soft Robot
SOURCE: https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1120196
Tesollo DG-5F-S Hand
SOURCE: https://en.tesollo.com/dg-5f-s/

🚨 Why It Matters
This is bigger than a few flashy robot demos. Humanoids are getting faster, more athletic, and more useful, while companies are also starting to build the manufacturing systems needed to produce them at real scale. At the same time, public safety, human-robot interaction, and real-world deployment are becoming much bigger issues as these machines move out of the lab and into everyday environments.

#ai #ainews #robots

_transcript: So, this week in robotics got kind of ridiculous. South Korea just showed off a humanoid that can run, jump, play soccer, and moonwalk. China is teaching humanoids to play tennis and even chase record-breaking sprint speeds. UB is now trying to mass-roduce 10,000 humanoid robots with semens. One restaurant robot turned a simple dance into total chaos. Another robot reads human brain signals to stop mistakes before they happen. A windpowered machine is trying to explore brutal terrain without batteries. Scientists built a swimming robot powered by self-trained living muscle. A fully compostable robot can survive over 1 million uses before breaking down in soil. And a new robotic hand is getting much closer to real human style dexterity. So yeah, this is one of those weeks where robotics kept dropping headline after headline. All right, let's start with this. Cast in South Korea just showed off its humanoid V0.7 and this thing looked way more athletic than most humanoids people are used to seeing. In the field test, the robot was running across a soccer pitch, jumping, taking shots on goal, and casually throwing in dance moves like a moonwalk. That alone makes the demo stand out because most humanoid videos still feel careful, slow, and a little stiff. This one looked fast, balanced, and actually confident. The robot weighs about 165 lbs or 75 kg, stands around 5'5, and was built by the dynamic robot control and design laboratory at KISS under Hwan Park. One of the biggest things here is that the team says it developed all the core parts itself, including the motors, motor drivers, and gearboxes. So, this is not just a flashy shell built around bot components. They are trying to own the full system. It uses a quasi direct drive setup with high torque motors and low gear ratios, which helps it react faster and move more smoothly. And it also has a custom 3K compound planetary gearbox designed to pack a lot of reduction into a compact single stage design. That setup gives it serious performance. The robot can already run at about 12 km per hour on flat ground and climb steps over 30 cm high. Park says the next goal is around 14 kmh. plus ladder climbing and getting over 40 cm steps. The knee actuator can hit 320 Newton meters of peak torque, while the ankle actuator is tuned for fast response and stability. On the software side, KISS trained it with deep reinforcement learning mixed with human motion data, which is why it moves in a much smoother, more natural way than a lot of AIdriven humanoids. The system also uses motor operating region modeling, so the simulation matches the real hardware, and the robot can even handle uneven terrain using propriception alone without depending on cameras. Case says the long-term goal is a full humanoid with an upper body that can work alongside people in industrial settings. And the lab is also building a framework called Doflow to let robots learn practical tasks directly from human demonstrations. Then you jump to a completely different idea. Cranfield University built a robot called Wanderbot that moves using wind instead of draining batteries. That sounds simple, though it is actually a pretty clever answer to a real problem. In many robotic systems, movement alone eats around 20% of the battery. That becomes a huge limitation for long missions in deserts, polar regions, or other planets. Wanderbot is a lowcost, modular, fully 3D printed robot designed for exactly those kinds of places. It uses a Savonius wind turbine and a Jansen linkage, the same multi-legged mechanism people know from Theo Jansen's StrandBon. The whole point is simplicity and repairability. Dr. Sarab Upadi described it as a first step towards self-sufficient robots that can go where humans cannot easily stay or maintain equipment for long. Because it is fully 3D printed, broken parts could theoretically be replaced on site instead of waiting for expensive resupply missions. That matters a lot in remote or extraterrestrial settings. Right now, it is still a low TRL prototype, though it already got attention at the European Space Ay's Astra Conference 2025. The next big step is maneuverability because the team still needs to teach it how to turn properly. Now, on the other side of the spectrum, robotics also gave us a perfect reminder that public deployment is still messy. A service robot at a Heidiow hot pot restaurant in Certino caused a chaotic scene after moving too close to diners and knocking dishes all over the place during a dance performance. In the video, the robot starts swinging its arms erratically, smashing plates, sending chopsticks and dishwear flying, and forcing staff members to rush in and physically stop it. One employee even appeared to look at her phone during the incident, likely trying to control or shut the robot down remotely. The machine is believed to be an Agibot X2, the same type shown at CES 2026 earlier this year. The reason people reacted so strongly is obvious. This was a hot pot restaurant, so there were boiling containers of soup sitting right on the tables. If the robot had knocked those over, this could have been much worse than a few broken dishes. Heidi Lao later told NBC News that the robot had not malfunctioned and that it had been brought too close to the table at a guest's request, which limited its movement. Maybe that is true, though it still points to the same issue. Robots that look great in controlled demos can become a problem fast in crowded, unpredictable, realworld spaces. Then there is sports. A team in China working with Galbat built a training system called Leighton that teaches humanoid robots to play tennis using imperfect human motion data. That is a big deal because robotic systems usually love perfect data and real life rarely gives you that. Instead of trying to capture everything with perfect detail, Leighton breaks tennis into smaller pieces like forehands, backhands, shuffles, and crossover steps. The team collected about 5 hours of motion data from amateur players using a compact motion capture setup, then used that to build a latent action space that helps the robot interpret and combine the motions more effectively. After that, reinforcement learning and large-scale simulation trained the system to react to incoming balls while keeping its movements natural. The final model was deployed on a Unitri G1 humanoid robot and in real world testing, it managed multi-shot rallies with humans from both fourcourt and backcourt positions. Across 10,000 trials, it reached a peak success rate of 96.5%, consistently returning balls near target locations. It still is not ready for full competitive play and right now it depends on motion capture in the real world. Though the researchers say future versions could use active vision and multi-agent training. The bigger point is that robots are now learning fast, dynamic sports from messy human data, and that could scale well beyond tennis into things like soccer and even parkour. At the same time, China's humanoid scene is also chasing outright speed. Unitry founder Wong Shing said humanoid robots may soon rival or even beat the fastest human ever in sprinting. That sounds crazy until you look at the numbers. In February, Jang University and Jingshi Technology revealed a full-size humanoid called Bolt that can hit 10 meters per second. For context, Usain Bolt's 100 meter world record averaged around 10.44 m/s. So, the gap is no longer massive. Wong even said that by around midyear, humanoid robots, especially in China, may run the 100 m in under 10 seconds. That is still a huge claim and there is a lot left to prove. High-speed bipeedal running is brutally difficult because everything has to stay perfectly synchronized. Balance, force, timing, sensing, and control all have to work together with almost no room for error. Wang also admitted that the biggest weakness in the whole field is still generalization. Robots can perform beautifully in controlled settings and then struggle badly when the world becomes unpredictable. That is still the hardest wall embodied AI has to get through. Then you have one of the strangest projects in the bunch and honestly one of the coolest. Researchers at the National University of Singapore built a fish inspired robot called Ostrobot powered by lab grown muscle that basically trains itself. The trick is that two engineered muscle tissues are connected so they pull against each other as they naturally contract during development. So instead of needing an outside system to train them, the muscles are effectively exercising themselves. That self-training approach produced a major jump in performance. Ostrobot reached 467 mm per minute, which the team says is the fastest ever reported for a skeletal muscle-driven robot. The trained muscles also achieved 7.05tonons 05 mton of maximum force and 8.51 mtons per square millimeter of stress, which is much stronger than what this field usually gets. The robot uses a single trained muscle to drive flexible tails and swims more than three times faster than versions powered by standard muscle tissue. Researchers could also control the robot using electrical signals and even trigger it to start and stop using sound cues like clapping. That makes it a lot more useful than older bio-hybrid robots that often looked weak or hard to control. Mass production is another huge theme. Now, UB signed a strategic cooperation agreement with Seaman's digital industry software to help scale humanoid robot production and reach 10,000 units per year in 2026. The deal was signed in Shenzhen on March 16th and combines UBC's robotics work with Seaman's experience in digital manufacturing, simulation, and industrial software. UB founder Joe Gian says orders have surged this year, and Reuters reported that total humanoid robot orders topped 1.4 billion yuan in 2025. This is where the humanoid race starts getting very real. Designing one impressive robot for a demo is one thing. Producing thousands of them reliably, affordably, and at high quality is something else entirely. Seammens is expected to help build the digital backbone for that push, covering everything from product design and simulation to process planning and manufacturing management. That may sound less exciting than a sprinting robot, though it is probably one of the most important shifts happening right now. This is the part where humanoids start trying to become an industry, not just a viral clip. Then there is Oklahoma State University where researchers are working on robots that can read human brain signals to catch mistakes before they happen. Their neuradaptive control system uses an EEG cap to detect error related potentials or ARPs, which are signals the brain produces the moment a person realizes something is going wrong, often before they physically react. Once the system detects that signal, the robot can slow down, stop, or hand back control within milliseconds. That matters a lot in dangerous environments like nuclear cleanup or deep sea inspections where a small mistake can turn into major damage fast. The team built an adaptive decoding model because everybody's brain signals are different. So, the system has to learn general patterns and then adjust to the user. They also use signal temporal logic as a safety framework. basically giving the robot a strict behavioral rulebook while still letting it respond to human brain signals. The testing is being done with NVIDIA Isaac Lab and Isaac Ross using RTX Pro 6000GPUs for realtime signal processing and simulation. Beyond industrial robotics, the same idea could eventually help prosthetics and exoskeletons respond much more naturally to what a user actually intends. Sustainability is starting to matter more, too. A team from Soul National University. So Gang University and Johannes Kepler University Lind developed what they describe as the first fully compostable soft robot that still delivers practical durability. The robot's frame uses poly or PGS, a biodegradable elastimemer with low hysteresus and strong elastic recovery. Its PGSbased bending actuator maintained performance over 1 million actuation cycles, which is a serious durability mark for something designed to eventually disappear. Even the electronics are biodegradable. Instead of normal metal and semiconductor parts, the team used biodegradable inorganic electronics that decompose along with the structure. Under industrial composting conditions, the whole system broke down within a few months and left no toxic residue. Plant growth tests even showed that the compost was safe and usable. The researchers also integrated sensors for curvature, strain, touch, temperature, humidity, and pH along with heaters, electrical stimulators, and drug delivery modules. All inside a single soft robotic finger. So, this is not some toy eco demo. It is a serious attempt to solve the waste problem robotics is going to face at scale. And finally, robotic hands. South Korean company Tasalo introduced a compact five-finger hand called DG5FS designed for humanoid and industrial systems. It has 20 degrees of freedom, measures 21 cm, and weighs just 880 g or about 1.94 lb. That is impressive because robotic hands are one of the toughest parts of humanoid design. They need dexterity, compliance, safety, and low weight all at the same time. And that is a brutal combination to get right. Talo says the hand uses back drivable joints which helps it absorb impacts and interact more safely with the world. And the company also offers a simpler 15 degree of freedom version for teams that want an easier control problem. At the same time, Samsung is building out its own hand lab and chasing tendon-driven designs with tactile sensing so robotic hands can detect pressure, texture, and tiny slips the way human hands do. That whole category is becoming extremely important, especially with Tesla, Figure, and everyone else pushing generalpurpose humanoids. Reports say the global market for humanoid five-finger robotic hands could hit $876 million by 2030. So, yeah, this was not a normal robotics week. Anyway, drop your take below, subscribe if you want more updates like this, and I'll catch you in the next one.
